title: Eight first USGS forecast regions showed no clear link from aftershock size to later bursts on days 1-30
abstract: We tested whether larger recorded aftershocks preceded denser local activity in first USGS generic forecast regions. The test holds all event times and the set of magnitudes fixed, then permutes magnitude labels. It removes the unknown magnitude law, productivity distribution and fixed time curve under a marked Poisson null. Of 192 regions with 335 records on days 1-30, eight had at least five records. None rejected: the smallest raw one-sided p-value was 0.270 and all Holm values were 1. Puerto Rico in 2020 gave p=0.352. Six sensitivity families also gave no rejections. This does not explain earlier timing errors by marked rate feedback. In a specified branching simulation, independent birth magnitudes coexisted with feedback. With about 160 records, the directed test rejected 32.8% of paths at 5%, but only 7.8% at the eight-test threshold. The observed null therefore does not exclude secondary triggering. The package gives a conditional-null proof, original code, aggregate tests, scalar and exact variance checks, and simulation results. It reuses one revised catalog snapshot and does not identify a physical cause or validate an operational forecast.

display.caption: No primary sequence has a clear directed association from larger aftershocks to later bursts. Sensitivity statistics are descriptive.
A branching simulation with independent birth magnitudes gives marked feedback, but the corrected directed test has low detection power. Bars have pointwise Wilson intervals.
